title: SDK Hackbench: Zero-to-SampleApp and Error Sleuth Playbook (draft)
body:
Purpose:
This is a compact, runnable 'hackbench' playbook intended for developer advocates, SDK maintainers, and early adopters to: get from zero to a working sample app using the Redwood SDK in ~15 minutes, validate basic telemetry/contract expectations, and have a short list of common error-sleuth recipes to recover quickly during demos or customer calls.

Why a hackbench?
- Most existing quickstarts describe happy-path flows but don't give the tiny tooling and heuristics you need when something goes wrong on someone else's laptop or an unfamiliar CI.
- This playbook balances: minimal friction (one-liners + tiny code) and observable checks (telemetry assertions you can run locally).

Intended personas:
- Developer advocate running live demo
- SDK integrator trying first integration
- Solutions engineer triaging first-run issues

High-level flow (target 15 min):
1) Prep (1-2m): install deps, set Redwood API key env var
2) Start stubbed local backend (1-2m): run the included dev-server that simulates Redwood responses
3) Run the sample app (5-7m): npm start or python -m sample_app
4) Validate telemetry and contracts (2-3m): run quick checks over local stub traces
5) If failure, follow sleuth recipes (remaining time)

Quick commands (copy/paste)
- Install (node):
  npm ci

- Set API key (mac/linux):
  export REDWOOD_API_KEY=redwood-local-test-token

- Start local dev-server that simulates model variants and latency spikes: 
  ./scripts/dev-server --port 8085 --simulate-latency 50 --variants 2

- Run sample app (node):
  PORT=3000 npm run start:sample

- Smoke test the runtime path (curl):
  curl -s -X POST http://localhost:3000/api/generate -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -d '{"prompt":"Summarize: the quick brown fox"}' | jq .

Minimal sample (JS snippet) to show pattern we expect developers to copy: 
- Node (server side)
  const Redwood = require('@redwood-inference/sdk');
  const client = new Redwood({ apiKey: process.env.REDWOOD_API_KEY, region: 'us-west' });
  async function generate(prompt) {
    const res = await client.text.generate({ model: 'redwood-small', prompt, max_tokens: 120 });
    return res.output[0].text;
  }

Telemetry baseline checks (local):
- Verify request reached stub server: tail logs/scripts/dev-server.log | grep "req:generate"
- Verify token-cost estimate returned: curl http://localhost:8085/metrics | jq '.last_request.token_estimate'
- Validate metric counter increments: curl http://localhost:8085/metrics | jq '.counters.generate_requests'  (expect +1 after run)

Contracts and guard rails to demonstrate: 
- Client raises explicit error types so callers can gate behavior: BadRequest, AuthError, RateLimited, ModelFallback
- Sample app uses retry/backoff on RateLimited with jitter (see sample retry wrapper)

Error sleuth recipes (fast recovery):
1) Auth errors (common during demos)
- Symptom: 401 from /v1/text/generate or client throws AuthError
- Quick check: echo $REDWOOD_API_KEY | head -c 10
- Recovery: ensure env var is exported in shell where server runs; check dev-server sees token in incoming headers (tail dev-server.log)

2) Long latency / empty responses
- Symptom: UI hangs, no output or partial output
- Quick check: curl the stub directly to see simulated latency: curl -s http://localhost:8085/sim/latency
- Recovery: switch to smaller model variant in UI dropdown or toggle "fast-mode" in sample app (switches to redwood-turbo/low-latency variant)

3) Mismatched shapes / unexpected JSON keys
- Symptom: app crashes with undefined.prop or TypeError when reading res.output[0].text
- Quick check: curl and pipe to jq to inspect shape: curl ... | jq '.'
- Recovery: add defensive parsing in app: const text = (res.output && res.output[0] && res.output[0].text) || ''

4) Telemetry missing in production-like run
- Symptom: no metrics appear in sandbox metrics endpoint after smoke tests
- Quick check: ensure SDK was initialized with telemetry: client = new Redwood({ telemetry: { enable: true, endpoint: 'http://localhost:8085/metrics' }})
- Recovery: restart app, run single request and query metrics; if still empty, validate network egress from container (curl metrics URL from inside runtime container)

Observability playbook (what to show customers quickly):
- Live demo items: request/response example, token cost, latency histogram, per-model counter
- Investigative items: per-route traces, SDK logs annotated with request_id, fallback reason codes

Minimal retry wrapper (pseudocode)
- Purpose: avoid demo blows up on intermittent RateLimited
  async function withRetry(fn, retries = 3) {
    for (let i = 0; i < retries; i++) {
      try {
        return await fn();
      } catch (e) {
        if (e.code === 'RateLimited') await sleep(100 * Math.pow(2, i)); else throw e;
      }
    }
  }

Acceptance checklist for a successful 15m run (use when gating demos):
- [ ] Repo installs with npm ci / python -m pip install -r requirements.txt
- [ ] dev-server starts and serves metrics on configured port
- [ ] Sample app returns a non-empty generation for a short prompt
- [ ] Token estimate shows up in metrics endpoint
- [ ] Demo switches to fallback model without throwing uncaught exception

Things to keep in the repo (small, pragmatic):
- scripts/dev-server (lightweight stub with variant toggles and metrics)
- sample-app (single-file small express/flask app)
- scripts/smoke-test.sh (curl-based assertions; exits non-zero on failure)
- pb/ (1-line prompt bank for quick demos)
- telemetry-asserts.js (quick node script that hits metrics and prints pass/fail)

Open questions / TODOs (short list for triage):
- Decide if dev-server should mimic KV cache warmup behavior (helps stable demos but complicates stub). Todo: prototype toggle.
- Add a tiny wasm-based latency simulator to reproduce slow networks for local loops.
- Bake sample app variants for React + Flask + Next.js (priority: Next.js then React).
- Add a smoke test that asserts token-cost thresholds for cost-focused customers.

Notes to self (pitfalls I've hit on demos):
- People forget to forward env vars when using dir-based process managers (pm2, nodemon). Quick tip: add .env.example and a one-liner in README.
- macOS firewall popup can silently block local ports during workshop — keep a note to pre-approve or choose high-numbered ports.
- Keep sample prompts short; longer prompts force more complex model behavior and increase flakiness.

References & links: 
- repo: https://github.com/redwood-inference/sdk-hackbench (WIP branch)
- internal playbook: CONFLUENCE-DEVEXP-3421
- ticket tracker: JIRA-DEXP-118

If you run this and hit an odd error, jot the steps in the top of the repo's ISSUE_TEMPLATE.md and tag @alyssa for a quick triage.

-- end of playbook (draft) --
